**Angiotensin Receptor–Neprilysin Inhibition in Heart Failure: A Narrative Review**

### Introduction
The management of heart failure (HF) has evolved dramatically over the last decade, transitioning from traditional neurohormonal blockade to advanced, multi-pathway modulation. Central to this therapeutic paradigm shift is the development of sacubitril/valsartan (originally known as LCZ696), the first-in-class angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI) [1]. For decades, renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors like angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) were the sole cornerstones of treatment [2]. Sacubitril/valsartan represents a critical breakthrough by combining a neprilysin inhibitor with an ARB, targeting complementary neurohormonal systems to improve cardiorenal outcomes [3].

### Pharmacological Mechanism of Action
Neprilysin is a neutral endopeptidase responsible for the degradation of several endogenous vasoactive peptides, including atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP), B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP), and C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) [1]. By inhibiting neprilysin, sacubitril (via its active metabolite LBQ657) increases the circulating levels of these peptides, which promote vasodilation, natriuresis, diuresis, and inhibit maladaptive cardiac hypertrophy and fibrosis [2]. However, because neprilysin also degrades angiotensin II, selective neprilysin inhibition leads to a counter-regulatory rise in vasoconstrictive angiotensin II. To mitigate this effect, valsartan is co-formulated to block the angiotensin II type 1 ($AT_1$) receptor [3]. The omission of an ACE-inhibiting component avoids the accumulation of bradykinin to levels that cause severe angioedema, making dual-acting ARNI therapy both highly efficacious and safer than historical vasopeptidase inhibitors [3].

### Clinical Evidence in Heart Failure with Reduced Ejection Fraction (HFrEF)
The clinical efficacy of sacubitril/valsartan in chronic HFrEF was established by the landmark PARADIGM-HF trial [3]. This prospective, randomized, double-blind trial compared sacubitril/valsartan (target dose 97/103 mg twice daily) against enalapril (target dose 10 mg twice daily) in 8,399 patients with stable HFrEF (LVEF ≤40%). The study was terminated early due to overwhelming clinical benefit: sacubitril/valsartan reduced the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization by 20% (hazard ratio [HR] 0.80, $P$<0.001) [3]. 

Subsequent analyses of PARADIGM-HF demonstrated that ARNI therapy significantly delayed clinical progression [4], maintained efficacy across all age groups [5], reduced sudden cardiac death and death from worsening heart failure [6], improved glycemic control in diabetic patients [7], and enhanced health-related quality of life and physical functioning [8,9]. Furthermore, sacubitril/valsartan preserved renal function, slowing the decline in estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) compared to enalapril [10]. 

Practical clinical implementation was supported by the TITRATION study, which showed that both conservative (6-week) and condensed (3-week) titration regimens are safe and well-tolerated [11]. In patients hospitalized for acute decompensated HF, the TRANSITION trial confirmed that pre-discharge initiation of sacubitril/valsartan is highly feasible and as well-tolerated as post-discharge initiation [12]. Crucially, the PIONEER-HF trial demonstrated that in-hospital initiation of sacubitril/valsartan in hemodynamically stabilized patients hospitalized with acute decompensated HFrEF significantly reduced NT-proBNP concentrations and decreased the risk of rehospitalization compared to enalapril [13].

Mechanistically, the PROVE-HF trial established a strong correlation between NT-proBNP reduction and reverse cardiac remodeling, demonstrating significant improvements in LVEF and ventricular volumes [14]. This was complemented by the EVALUATE-HF trial, which highlighted early improvements in left ventricular volumes and left atrial volume index [15]. Additionally, the PRIME trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan is superior to valsartan in reducing functional mitral regurgitation severity [16]. However, the limits of this therapy were highlighted in the LIFE trial, where sacubitril/valsartan did not show superior clinical or biomarker efficacy over valsartan in patients with highly advanced, end-stage HFrEF [17].

### Efficacy Across the Ejection Fraction Spectrum
Expanding the use of sacubitril/valsartan to heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) was investigated in the PARAGON-HF trial [18]. In this trial comparing sacubitril/valsartan with valsartan in 4,822 patients with LVEF ≥45%, the ARNI narrowly missed statistical significance for the primary composite endpoint of cardiovascular death and total HF hospitalizations (rate ratio 0.87, $P$=0.059) [18]. Nonetheless, prespecified subgroup analyses revealed a distinct treatment benefit in women [19] and in patients with lower LVEF ranges. A subsequent pooled analysis of PARADIGM-HF and PARAGON-HF confirmed that the clinical benefits of sacubitril/valsartan extend up to an LVEF of approximately 55% to 60%, establishing its utility in patients with HFmrEF [20]. This was supported by the PARAGLIDE-HF trial, which demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP compared to valsartan in patients with LVEF >40% stabilized after a worsening HF event [21]. Additionally, the PARALLAX trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan significantly reduced NT-proBNP levels compared to individualized medical therapy in patients with HFpEF [22]. A recent meta-analysis confirmed that sacubitril/valsartan improves NYHA class and health status in HFmrEF and HFpEF cohorts [23].

### Extra-Cardiac, Cognitive, and Special Populations
The cardiorenal benefits of sacubitril/valsartan were explored in chronic kidney disease (CKD). In the UK HARP-III trial, sacubitril/valsartan had similar effects on kidney function to irbesartan over 12 months, but demonstrated superior blood pressure lowering and reduction in cardiac biomarkers [24]. Regarding cognitive safety, because neprilysin degrades amyloid-beta in the brain, concerns had been raised about potential cognitive decline. However, a detailed analysis of PARAGON-HF established that sacubitril/valsartan does not cause cognitive decline or accelerate amyloid-beta deposition in the brain compared to valsartan [25].

In the post-myocardial infarction setting, the PARADISE-MI trial showed that sacubitril/valsartan was not associated with a significantly lower rate of CV death or incident HF compared to ramipril, indicating that routine post-MI initiation is not warranted in the absence of clinical HF [26], though select patients may still derive remodeling benefits [27]. In pediatric patients with systemic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, the PANORAMA-HF trial demonstrated that sacubitril/valsartan had comparable safety and clinical efficacy to enalapril [28].

### Guidelines and Clinical Application
Current major clinical guidelines, including those of the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) [29] and the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA) [30], have integrated these findings. Sacubitril/valsartan is recommended as a Class I first-line therapy to replace ACE inhibitors or ARBs in symptomatic patients with HFrEF [29, 30]. For patients with HFmrEF and HFpEF with LVEF below normal, it is also recommended to reduce hospitalization and mortality (Class IIb) [30], underscoring its pivotal role across the heart failure spectrum.
